The infusion pump in bay four beeped, and Jaya froze. "I learned this setup last month," she whispered. "It's gone. I'm useless."
Uma, the senior nurse on the ward, pulled a worn pocket notebook from her scrubs. "Page twelve. I wrote it after my own training, because I knew I'd lose it too." Together they ran the steps, checking each one aloud.
Later, in the staff room, Uma showed Jaya the reminder on her phone: first Friday of every month, twenty minutes with the practice pump in the skills room. "The brain throws out what it doesn't use. That's housekeeping, not failure. So I bring back the things that matter before they fade."
Jaya copied page twelve into her own notebook and booked a Friday slot.

qa.q: Where did Uma keep the steps for the pump setup?
qa.a: In a worn pocket notebook, on page twelve, which she wrote after her own training.

qa.q: Why does forgetting not frighten Uma the way it frightens Jaya?
qa.a: Uma sees forgetting as the brain throwing out what it doesn't use, like housekeeping, so a blank moment feels expected rather than a sign of failure.

qa.q: What small steps help Jaya after this shift?
qa.a: Copying page twelve into her own notebook and booking a Friday practice slot, so the setup is refreshed before it fades.

qa.q: How might Jaya's view of herself change after hearing Uma?
qa.a: Jaya may stop reading a blank moment as proof she is useless, since even a senior nurse plans for forgetting.

grounding: A working nurse keeps written notes, practises a rarely used skill on a monthly schedule, and calls forgetting ordinary housekeeping rather than failure.

Subject: Re: I forgot everything from training

Hi Mridul,

Your message made me laugh, kindly. Three months into my job I blanked on a spreadsheet formula I'd used fifty times in college. I sat there feeling like a fraud.

Here's what I do now. I keep one plain notes file called 'how I did it', with every fiddly step written in my own words. Every second Sunday I open it and redo two or three items from scratch, the ones I'd need in a crunch. The rest I let go.

Your head isn't leaking. It's sorting: keeping what you use, dropping what you don't. The notes and the Sunday reruns are just how you tell it what to keep.

Try it for a month and tell me how it goes.

Eshaan

qa.q: What is the name of Eshaan's notes file?
qa.a: It is called 'how I did it'.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel after blanking on the formula, and how does it seem now?
qa.a: Eshaan felt like a fraud at the time, but now sees the blank as the mind sorting, so the memory brings a kind laugh instead of shame.

qa.q: What would you advise Mridul to do in the first month, based on this email?
qa.a: Start the notes file while training is fresh, then pick a fixed day to redo a few key tasks, the way Eshaan does every second Sunday.

qa.q: What might it be like for Mridul to read this reply?
qa.a: Mridul will probably feel relieved that a friend forgot things too, and glad to have a plan instead of a worry. 😊

grounding: A young employee writes a friend about keeping step-by-step notes, redoing key tasks every second Sunday, and seeing forgetting as the mind sorting.

passage:
Dilnaz, you know the croissant disaster? Last winter I hadn't made laminated dough for four months, and on the big order day my hands just didn't know it. I kept folding in the wrong order. I went home thinking, that's it, I'm losing it.
Then my old instructor rang and said something simple. "Zeenat, you're not losing it. Your brain made room for the cakes you bake every day." Made sense.
So now I keep this little recipe diary, grease stains and all. And on the first Monday of every month, before the shop opens, I do one practice batch of whatever I haven't touched in a while. Some months it's dough, sometimes piping.
Honestly? Forgetting doesn't scare me now. It's just my cue to open the diary.

qa.q: What did Zeenat keep getting wrong on the big order day?
qa.a: Zeenat kept folding the laminated dough in the wrong order after four months without making it.

qa.q: What was Zeenat afraid of after that order day?
qa.a: Zeenat feared losing the skill for good, reading one blank day as proof of decline.

qa.q: Which habit keeps Zeenat's rarer skills ready, and why does it work?
qa.a: A practice batch on the first Monday of every month, guided by the recipe diary, brings back a skill before it fades completely.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz take the croissant story?
qa.a: Dilnaz might find it funny and reassuring, and see that forgetting a skill can be handled with a diary and practice rather than panic.

grounding: A working baker keeps a recipe diary, practises neglected skills monthly, and treats forgetting as the brain making room rather than failure.

passage:
Rain hammered the bus-stop roof, and the school bus was already twenty minutes late. Tanvir kicked a puddle.
"At my old school the bus was never late," Tanvir told Damini, the girl from the new class who shared the shelter. "And everybody was friends. Nobody ever fought."
Damini shrugged. "Nobody?"
"Nobody. It was the best class in the world."
While digging for a dry handkerchief, Tanvir pulled out an old rough notebook. On the back page, in big angry letters: NEVER SHARING MY TIFFIN WITH THAT BENCH AGAIN!! Below it was a drawing of a cross face.
Tanvir stared at it, then quickly shut the notebook. "That was just one day," Tanvir mumbled, as the bus splashed round the corner.

qa.q: What was written on the back page of Tanvir's old notebook?
qa.a: NEVER SHARING MY TIFFIN WITH THAT BENCH AGAIN!!, with a drawing of a cross face below it.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir insist the old class never fought?
qa.a: Tanvir misses the old school and feels unsettled in the new one, so from far away the old class feels perfect and the quarrels have faded.

qa.q: How could a parent help Tanvir without arguing?
qa.a: They could say it's fine to miss old friends, then ask about an ordinary day there, good and grumpy bits, and about one nice thing in the new class. 🙂

qa.q: How might Damini feel hearing that the old class was the best in the world?
qa.a: Damini might feel the new class is being compared unfairly, or that Tanvir isn't ready to give it a chance yet.

grounding: A child who changed schools calls the old class perfect until an angry note in an old notebook shows the forgotten quarrels.

Vinita pressed her forehead against the balcony grille of their new flat in Bengaluru, watching the colony kids play cricket below.
"In Kolkata, my class was like a family," she said. "We did everything together. Sports day, tiffin, everything."
Her little brother Tejas looked up from his jigsaw. "You cried about Mouli every week. She said your drawing was ugly."
"That never happened."
"And the time the whole class blamed you for the broken window."
Vinita opened her mouth, then closed it. She did remember the window, a little: standing alone by the staff room, cheeks hot.
"It was still nice," she said, quieter.
"Some of it," Tejas agreed, and fitted in a piece.
Downstairs, a girl waved up at the balcony. Vinita hesitated, then waved back.

qa.q: Which city did Vinita's family move from?
qa.a: Kolkata; they now live in a new flat in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What does Vinita's quieter 'It was still nice' suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She is starting to recall the hard moments too, and feels a mix of missing her old class and admitting it wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What could help Vinita settle into the colony?
qa.a: Saying yes to small chances like the girl's wave, and letting herself miss Kolkata while giving new friends a fair try.

qa.q: How does Tejas see his sister's story about Kolkata?
qa.a: Tejas remembers the weekly tears and the window blame, so to him 'like a family' leaves a lot out.

grounding: A girl who moved cities remembers her old class as a family, and her brother reminds her of quarrels she has smoothed away.

Hansa, sit with your Dada. You look the way I looked at fifteen, before my board exams.
Back then I would lie on the roof and think, if only I were six again. At six I flew kites all day, no books, no marks. Life was one long holiday, I told myself.
Then one evening my mother heard me moaning about it. She laughed. "Santosh, at six you were terrified of the dark. You cried every night the power went. And you begged to cross the road alone, and I never let you."
I had forgotten all of it. The kite days were true, but so was the dark.
I'm not saying exams are easy. I'm saying the old days weren't only kites. Now, show me which chapter is giving you trouble.

qa.a: The dark; he cried every night the power went.

qa.q: Why did fifteen-year-old Santosh long to be six again?
qa.a: With board exams pressing, the kite-flying days felt like one long holiday, a comfort compared with books and marks.

qa.q: How does Dada turn the memory into help for Hansa?
qa.a: He admits exams are hard, shows the past had its own fears, then moves straight to the difficult chapter, so the pressure gets tackled instead of escaped.

qa.a: She probably found it sweet and a little funny, since she remembered the nightly tears and the limits he had forgotten.

passage:
The power went out at nine, with Zeenat's project due at midnight and the laptop on eleven percent.
Zeenat lit the emergency lamp and flopped onto the bed. Across the room, Dilnaz, her eight-year-old sister, was happily colouring by lamplight.
"You're so lucky," Zeenat said. "I'd give anything to be eight. No deadlines. Just crayons and cartoons."
Dilnaz looked up. "I have a spelling test tomorrow. And I can't reach the top shelf. And you won't let me walk to the shop alone."
"That's different."
"And I'm scared of the dark," Dilnaz added, edging her lamp closer.
Zeenat remembered, suddenly, hiding under a blanket during power cuts at that age, heart thumping.
She sat up, opened the laptop, dimmed the screen, and typed the conclusion first.

qa.q: How much battery did Zeenat's laptop have when the power went out?
qa.a: Eleven percent, with the project due at midnight.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat wish she were eight again tonight?
qa.a: The deadline and the power cut make her feel trapped, so childhood looks like only crayons and cartoons, without the fears she once had. 😅

qa.q: What sensible step does Zeenat take once she stops wishing?
qa.a: She dims the screen to save battery and writes the conclusion first, working with the time and power she actually has.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see being eight?
qa.a: To Dilnaz, eight comes with its own worries: a spelling test, shelves out of reach, rules about the shop, and fear of the dark.

grounding: A teenager under deadline pressure envies her little sister's carefree age until the sister's own fears remind her what childhood was like.

passage:
Between school and evening coaching, Sonali had exactly forty minutes. She spent them on the floor of the Andheri flat, flipping through an old photo album.
There she was at five, chocolate on her chin, grinning at a birthday party. "Look at me," she said to Saurabh, her older brother, who was eating toast in the doorway. "Not a single worry. Why can't life be like that again?"
Saurabh leaned over and turned the page. Sonali, same age, howling on the edge of a swimming pool, clutching the rail.
"You screamed through every lesson that summer," he said. "And you cried when Mummy wouldn't let you go to the park without her."
Sonali frowned at the photo. She had forgotten the pool entirely.
"Still," she said, "it looks easier."
"Some of it was," Saurabh said. "Your bag's by the door."
She closed the album gently, not quite ready to put it away.

qa.q: What was Sonali doing in the swimming pool photo?
qa.a: Howling on the edge of a swimming pool, clutching the rail.

qa.q: Why does Sonali want life to be like it was at five?
qa.a: Squeezed between school and coaching, she longs for the carefree feeling in the birthday photo; the album is a comfort from the pressure.

qa.q: What could help Sonali with the pressure itself, not just the longing?
qa.a: Telling her family how packed her days feel and finding small breaks now, instead of looking for ease only in the past.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see Sonali's 'not a single worry' claim?
qa.a: Saurabh remembers the screaming at swimming lessons and the park rules, so he sees her early years as happy but not worry-free.

grounding: A busy teenager longs for her early childhood through photos, forgetting its fears until her brother turns the page.

Dear Bhavna,

Writing this at 1 a.m. from hostel room 214, because the lab report is due tomorrow and I can't face it.

Do you remember our school canteen? The samosas, the terrace where we did nothing for hours? Everything there was so easy. At home Amma had dinner ready, the fan worked, nobody expected me to understand thermodynamics.

Here the mess dal is water and my roommate plays music till two. I've been going home every weekend. Three weekends in a row now. I tell myself it's to see Amma.

Honestly, I think I also go so I don't have to sit in the study group, where everyone seems to know more than me.

Tell me I'm not the only one.

Missing you, and home, and everything,
Minakshi

Every evening around seven, out comes the phone, and it's the same video: a courtyard in Jodhpur, a grandmother laughing, a cousin's scooter. Jagdish watches it twice, sometimes three times.

Day centre supervisor's note, Thursday

Mr Bhupen, one of our regulars, spent most of lunch telling Sabina, our new activities coordinator, how much better life was in the sixties. "Doors unlocked, milk delivered, children respected elders. We were poor but happy."
Sabina has read the history. The sixties also meant ration queues, and Mr Bhupen himself once told us about walking miles for water. I watched Sabina's face; there was a flicker, as if a correction was coming.
It didn't come. Sabina asked, "What did the milk taste like?" and he talked for ten minutes, smiling.
Afterwards Sabina told me, "The hardship was real, but so is what he misses. I don't need to win that one."
Next step: I've asked Sabina to start a Thursday memory circle.

qa.q: What question did Sabina ask Mr Bhupen?
qa.a: "What did the milk taste like?"

qa.q: What does the flicker on Sabina's face suggest, and why did no correction come?
qa.a: Sabina seemed tempted to mention the ration queues, but decided the warmth of his memory mattered more than winning the point.

qa.q: Why is the supervisor's next step a good one?
qa.a: A Thursday memory circle gives the elders a regular place to share memories and lets Sabina keep building trust by listening.

qa.q: How might Mr Bhupen have felt if Sabina had corrected him?
qa.a: He might have felt dismissed or foolish, and been less willing to talk with Sabina again.

grounding: A young coordinator hears an elder praise the sixties, knows the era was hard, and chooses kind listening over correction.

Sunday, 11 p.m.

Big family lunch at Sarika Mami's today. By dessert she was off again: "In our time, families ate together every night, no phones, no stress, everyone respected each other."

My fingers itched to reply. I know from Amma that Mami's own mother-in-law barely let her speak at that table, and that they cooked for twenty with no fridge. "No stress" is quite a claim.

But I watched Mami's face while she talked. Soft. Like she was sitting in that old kitchen again. Whatever else was true, that warmth was true too.

So I just said, "Tell me about the Diwali lunches," and she did, for half an hour. Amma winked at me across the table.

Still think those years were tougher than she says. Didn't need to say it today.
Lavanya

qa.q: What did Lavanya ask Sarika Mami to talk about?
qa.a: The Diwali lunches.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya's fingers itch to reply?
qa.a: Lavanya knew about the strict mother-in-law and cooking for twenty with no fridge, so 'no stress' felt untrue and tempting to correct.

qa.q: Which choice did Lavanya make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Lavanya asked for a story instead of arguing, which honoured Mami's warm memory and kept the lunch friendly.

qa.q: What might Amma's wink mean?
qa.a: Amma probably appreciated that Lavanya let Mami enjoy the memory instead of starting a debate at the table. 😊

grounding: A young adult listens to an aunt's golden picture of the past, sees both the warmth and the hardship, and keeps the peace by listening.

passage:
Last month I went back to Siliguri for the first time in six years, and I was sure I'd return to Pune miserable.
I walked past our old rented house, the tea stall, the school gate. My chest ached in the best way. Baba used to buy me, his only daughter, hot jalebis at that stall. Arnab, my brother, and I would race home in the rain.
On the train back, I caught myself thinking: life was so much sweeter then. So I made myself finish the thought honestly. The roof leaked every monsoon. Baba lost his job the year I was nine, and I remember the silence at dinner.
Both are true. The sweetness taught me to make small treats matter, which I still do. The hard parts remind me that my small flat in Pune, with its steady roof, is not nothing.
That's how I keep the old days now: as a warm shawl, not a measuring stick.
Kalyani

qa.q: Which town did Kalyani visit for the first time in six years?
qa.a: Siliguri.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling as she walked past the old house and tea stall?
qa.a: Her chest ached in the best way: a warm, sweet longing for the childhood with Baba and Arnab. 🤍

qa.q: How does Kalyani stop the trip from making Pune feel poor?
qa.a: She finishes the thought honestly, recalling the leaking roof and Baba's lost job, and keeps the lesson of small treats, so the past is comfort, not a measuring stick.

qa.q: How might Arnab remember the same childhood?
qa.a: Arnab might also treasure racing home in the rain, and could carry his own memories of the leaks and the quiet dinners that year.

passage:
Mentoring notes, Maria, programme coordinator

Tanuja came back from her college reunion glowing. In our check-in she showed me photos: the old canteen, the debate trophy, her classmates in matching kurtas. "I felt twenty again," she said.

Then she added something I wrote down. "On the bus I started thinking our college team was better than my team here. So I made a list of what was hard then too: the exam panic, the hostel curfew, the friend I fell out with. That helped."

She said she wants to bring the reunion spirit into work, not measure work against it. Her idea: a short Friday story circle where volunteers share one good memory and one lesson.

What I did next: approved a trial of three Fridays, and asked her to lead the first.

qa.q: What idea did Tanuja bring back from the reunion?
qa.a: A short Friday story circle where volunteers share one good memory and one lesson.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja make a list on the bus?
qa.a: She noticed herself thinking the college team was better than her team now, and wanted an honest picture so the past wouldn't spoil the present.

qa.q: What makes Tanuja's approach a healthy use of nostalgia?
qa.a: She enjoys the reunion glow and turns it into something useful at work, while the list of hard things stops unfair comparisons.

qa.q: How does Maria respond to Tanuja's glow?
qa.a: Maria takes it seriously, writes down her words, approves a three-Friday trial and trusts Tanuja to lead the first.

grounding: A coordinator records how a young woman enjoys reunion memories, lists what was hard back then, and brings the good spirit into her current work.

grounding: An older sibling watches an upset younger brother list only the week's bad events and predict a bad tomorrow, forgetting a recent prize.

passage:
Monday. Mohit laughed when Divyansh slipped in the corridor, and Divyansh stopped speaking to him. At home he flung his bag down. "This whole week is rubbish. Tomorrow will be rubbish." He couldn't think of one nice thing, not even last Friday's samosa party.
Wednesday. Divyansh sat alone at lunch, sure the maths test would go wrong. It went fine, but he told Nani it was "probably bad."
Saturday. Mohit knocked on the door with a borrowed comic and a sorry. They sat on the steps reading. "Remember the samosa party?" Mohit said, and Divyansh laughed. Suddenly he remembered the sunny PT period and his gold star too. "Huh," he said. "It wasn't all rubbish."

qa.q: What did Mohit bring on Saturday?
qa.a: A borrowed comic and a sorry.

qa.q: Why couldn't Divyansh think of one nice thing on Monday?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry after Mohit laughed, and that sad mood let only bad memories come to mind.

qa.q: What could help Divyansh on a day like Monday?
qa.a: Waiting until he feels calmer, or looking for one good thing from the week, like the samosa party, before deciding the whole week is rubbish.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt hearing the test was 'probably bad'?
qa.a: Nani may have worried, not knowing the test went fine and that his mood was doing the talking.

grounding: Across several days, an upset child sees only bad memories and expects a bad tomorrow, until making up with a friend brings the good ones back.

passage:
Ankita, you've got a face like a rainy day. Let your grandpa tell you something.
When I was ten, in Goa, my best friend moved away to Mumbai. That evening my mother asked how school was. I told her everything was terrible: the teacher hated me, I'd failed my sums, and the monsoon had ruined football. "Tomorrow will be worse," I said.
My mother just said, "Francis, write down the whole week tonight. Good and bad." I sat with the paper, and slowly it came back: nine out of ten in sums. The teacher had let me ring the bell. We'd played football in the rain, laughing.
I was still sad about my friend. But the week wasn't what my sadness said it was.
Now. What happened today?

qa.q: Where did young Francis's best friend move?
qa.a: To Mumbai.

qa.q: Why did ten-year-old Francis think tomorrow would be worse?
qa.a: Sad about losing his friend, he could only recall bad things, so the future looked bad too.

qa.q: Why did his mother's idea help, and could Ankita use it?
qa.a: Writing down the good and the bad brought forgotten good moments back; Ankita could try the same with today.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Ankita might feel understood and less alone, and more ready to tell grandpa about today. 🙂

grounding: A grandfather recalls being a sad ten-year-old who remembered only a bad week and expected worse, until writing it all down showed the good parts.

passage:
Dear Yamini Didi,

You asked me to write when things felt heavy. They do.

Yesterday Kiran texted "ok" when I asked about cricket on Sunday. Just "ok." I've read it maybe twenty times. It must mean he's fed up with me. And in the chemistry test I got 14 out of 25, which proves I'm hopeless at everything. When I try to think of anything I've done right this year, my head goes blank.

It's been like this for weeks, not days. I don't know if "ok" really means anything. Maybe it only feels true because I feel low.

Mummy noticed I've gone quiet at dinner. She's asked the school counsellor to see me on Thursday. I said I'd go.

Write back soon.
Ramesh

qa.q: What did Kiran text when Ramesh asked about cricket?
qa.a: Just "ok."

qa.q: Why does Ramesh read 'ok' as a sign Kiran is fed up?
qa.a: Weeks of low mood make everything look like rejection and failure, so a plain reply feels like proof, even though Ramesh half suspects the mood is shaping it.

qa.q: What is a wise next step, and who is already helping?
qa.a: Seeing the school counsellor on Thursday, as Mummy arranged, and keeping Yamini Didi in the loop; weeks of low mood deserve that kind of care.

qa.q: How might Kiran have meant that text?
qa.a: Kiran may simply have been busy or agreeing to Sunday; the short reply could be completely neutral.

grounding: A teenager in a weeks-long low mood reads a neutral text as rejection and recalls only failures, while a parent arranges counsellor support.

passage:
Madhuri, don't laugh, okay? The group chat went quiet after I posted my painting. Two hours, nothing. I just know everyone thinks it's bad. Then Sir wrote "Vandana, see me after class" on my essay, and I'm sure it's because it's terrible. Everything I've done this term has flopped. The debate, the maths quiz, all of it.
You say Sir only wanted to talk about the art competition? Maybe. I don't know. My brain keeps saying it's bad news.
It's been weeks, honestly. I wake up already tired, and things I loved feel grey.
You think I should tell someone? My Chachi is easy to talk to. And the counsellor has that open hour on Fridays.
Okay. If you come with me on Friday, I'll go.

qa.q: What did Sir write on Vandana's essay?
qa.a: "Vandana, see me after class."

qa.q: Why is Vandana so sure the quiet group chat means the painting is bad?
qa.a: Weeks of low mood make silence and neutral notes feel like rejection, and the mind serves up only past flops as evidence.

qa.q: What plan does Vandana agree to, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Going to the counsellor's Friday open hour with Madhuri and perhaps talking to Chachi; weeks of feeling grey deserve care from trusted adults.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see the quiet group chat?
qa.a: Madhuri probably thinks people were just busy, and may be worried that Vandana has felt low for so long.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend how silence and a teacher's note feel like rejection during weeks of low mood, then agrees to seek adult help.

passage:
Kunal used to be the loudest one in the dressing room. This month he's different, and I'm not sure what's going on inside him.
On Tuesday Coach posted the team list with Kunal as substitute. Most of us are subs sometimes. Kunal read it and said, "Coach has given up on me." Then he listed every missed goal since June, like he'd kept a diary of them.
When I texted him "see you at practice", he replied, "Why, so you can laugh?" I wasn't laughing. I just meant see you.
I'm Samir, just his mate, not a doctor. But this has gone on for weeks. So I told Coach quietly after practice. Coach thanked me, said they'd call Kunal's parents that evening, and asked me to keep being a friend.

qa.q: What did Kunal reply when Samir texted 'see you at practice'?
qa.a: "Why, so you can laugh?"

qa.q: Why does being a substitute feel like proof to Kunal that Coach has given up?
qa.a: His low mood makes a normal team decision read as rejection and pulls up every missed goal as evidence, so the judgment feels like fact.

qa.q: Was Samir right to tell Coach? Why?
qa.a: Yes; the low mood had lasted weeks, and a caring adult can involve Kunal's parents and get proper help, while Samir keeps being a friend.

qa.q: What is it like for Samir to get that text?
qa.a: Samir feels misread, having only meant see you, and worried about how different Kunal has become.

grounding: A teammate notices a teenager reading neutral messages as rejection and recalling only failures for weeks, and tells a caring adult.

passage:
Supervisor's note, internship programme, week 6. Hrithik

Tejas had a brilliant Monday: the client loved the prototype and the whole team cheered. By Tuesday evening Tejas had volunteered for the weekend hackathon, offered to redo the onboarding slides, agreed to mentor two first-years, and planned to cycle to the office on the flooded route "because it'll be fine".
I asked how the college assignments due Friday fit in. A long pause. "Oh. I forgot those."
Nothing is wrong with enthusiasm, and the good mood was earned. But the yeses came faster than the checking.
What I did next: sat with Tejas and listed every commitment with its hours. Tejas dropped the slides and the hackathon, kept one mentee, and took the bus. We agreed on a rule: sleep on any new yes.

qa.q: How many first-years did Tejas agree to mentor?
qa.a: Two first-years.

qa.q: Why did the flooded cycle route seem fine to Tejas?
qa.a: After the client loved the prototype, Tejas felt on top of the world, and that glow made risks look small and every yes feel easy.

qa.q: What rule did they agree on, and why does it help?
qa.a: Sleep on any new yes; a night's pause lets the checking catch up with the good mood.

qa.q: How does Hrithik view Tejas's burst of yeses?
qa.a: Hrithik sees the enthusiasm as earned and welcome, but worries the commitments outran the checking, especially with assignments due Friday.

grounding: A supervisor records how an intern's great mood led to too many yeses and a risky commute, and how they slowed down together.

passage:
Friday night!! 🎉

Best day of the year. Got the lead in the college play AND my scholarship renewal came through. I felt like I could fly.

So when Hemant asked if I'd drive his dad's car to the lake at midnight with the whole gang, I said yes before he finished. Also said yes to the fest committee, to tutoring Hemant's cousin every morning, and to a Sunday trek that's supposed to be "moderate" (it isn't, I checked later).

Just looked at my calendar. Rehearsals start Monday. Quiz on Tuesday. I've driven at night exactly once, on a practice round, and it was scary.

Why did all of it sound so easy at 5 p.m.? Everything looked shiny.

Tomorrow: tell Hemant I'm not driving. Keep the play, keep the committee. The rest can wait.
Raghav

qa.q: What two pieces of good news did Raghav get?
qa.a: The lead in the college play and the scholarship renewal.

qa.q: Why did the midnight drive sound easy to Raghav at 5 p.m.?
qa.a: The joy of the day made everything look shiny, so a night drive felt like fun rather than a risk for someone who had driven at night only once. 😅

qa.q: Which of Raghav's plans for tomorrow is wisest, and why?
qa.a: Telling Hemant no to the night drive, because it is the riskiest yes; keeping only the play and the committee also protects rehearsals and the quiz.

qa.q: How might Hemant react when Raghav backs out of driving?
qa.a: Hemant might be disappointed at first, but could also be relieved that his dad's car won't be driven at night by someone so new to it.

grounding: A student on a joyful day says yes to a risky night drive and too many plans, then sees the risks once the glow fades.

passage:
Monday, 7 p.m. Rekha sat in her car in the office car park, jaw tight. In the review meeting, Charu had presented Rekha's research as the team's idea without a word of credit. Rekha typed a resignation email on her phone, thumbs stabbing. Her thumb hovered over send. Then she moved it to drafts and wrote on a sticky note: "Decide Thursday."
Tuesday. She went for a long walk after work and told her sister the whole story, loudly.
Thursday morning. Coffee, calm, the draft open. Half of it still rang true: she did want credit. The other half, quitting a job she mostly liked, didn't. She deleted it and wrote instead: "Charu, can we talk about how research is credited in future reviews?"
Charu replied within an hour: "Yes. Sorry, that was careless of me."

qa.q: What did Rekha write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Decide Thursday."

qa.q: What does Rekha's thumb hovering over send, then moving to drafts, suggest?
qa.a: She was furious and felt the resignation was right, yet sensed her anger might be choosing for her, so she wanted a calmer self to decide.

qa.q: Why did waiting until Thursday work for Rekha?
qa.a: Once calm, she could separate the true part, wanting credit, from the angry part, quitting, and send a message that fixed the real problem.

qa.q: How might Charu see Rekha's Thursday message?
qa.a: Charu likely reads it as calm and fair, which makes it easier to admit the mistake and apologise instead of getting defensive.

grounding: Over several days, a young woman drafts a resignation in anger, delays it, and returns calm to find her view has changed.

passage:
Minakshi, you've been typing and deleting that message for ten minutes. Let your Nani tell you something from when I was about your age.
I was twenty-four, just married, working at the post office. One night after a terrible fight at home, I sat down to write to my father: I was coming back, the marriage was a mistake. Pages of it.
At the post office, where everyone called me Sharmila-di, we had a saying: never post a letter written at midnight. So I put it under my pillow.
Three days later I read it with a cup of tea. Some of it was still true; we did need to talk about money and his mother's rules. But the "coming back" part? That was the anger talking. I tore it up, and we talked instead. That's how your Nana and I managed forty years.
So. Save it. Read it when you're calm.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila work at twenty-four?
qa.a: At the post office.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila put the letter under her pillow instead of posting it?
qa.a: She sensed that her anger that night was writing the letter, and wanted to see whether it still felt true once she was calm.

qa.q: What is Sharmila advising Minakshi to do, and why?
qa.a: Save the message and read it again when calm, so a passing mood doesn't make the decision.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's father have been affected if the letter had arrived?
qa.a: He would likely have been alarmed and worried by a sudden 'coming back' over a fight she later worked out.

grounding: A grandmother recalls holding back an angry midnight letter at twenty-four and rereading it calm, and passes the habit to her grandchild.

passage:
The offer email said: reply by 9 a.m. tomorrow. It was 11 p.m., the power had gone, and Neelam sat on the floor with her phone at thirty percent, still stinging from that afternoon's rejection by the company she'd wanted most.
"Just take the Nagpur job," she muttered. "Nobody else wants me." She started typing yes.
Then she stopped. Nobody else wants me. She'd felt exactly that after her first internship fell through, and it hadn't been true then either.
She called Swati instead. "I'm in a pit tonight. Don't let me decide anything."
"Then don't," Swati said. "Ask them for two days."
Neelam wrote one line to the recruiter asking for Monday, sent it, and switched the phone off.
On Monday, rested, she read the offer again. The pay was fair, but the role wasn't in her field. She declined politely and kept applying.

qa.q: What deadline did the offer email give?
qa.a: Reply by 9 a.m. tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Neelam notice about the thought 'Nobody else wants me'?
qa.a: She recognised it as the despair of the rejection talking, the same feeling she had after her first internship fell through, which hadn't been true then either.

qa.q: How did Neelam handle the time pressure wisely?
qa.a: She asked the recruiter for more time and switched off the phone, so she could decide on Monday when rested and calm.

qa.q: How does Swati see her part that night?
qa.a: Swati doesn't try to solve anything; she backs Neelam's wish not to decide while low and suggests asking for two days. 🤍

grounding: Under a tight deadline and a power cut, a young woman notices her despair, delays a major job decision, and decides differently once calm.
